title: Moving to per-second billing on StarSling Runners
summary: StarSling Runners now bill by the second with no one-minute minimum. We estimate customers save up to 25% on runner compute from per-second billing alone.
body_markdown:
[StarSling Runners](https://starsling.dev/products/runners) now bill by the second. Every job is metered in whole seconds from job start to finish, with no one-minute minimum. We estimate customers save **up to 25%** on runner compute from per-second billing alone.


[GitHub-hosted runners](https://docs.github.com/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing) and most CI runner providers round every job up to the next whole minute. A 15-second lint check bills as a full minute. A 1m 05s test job bills as two.


On StarSling, you now pay for the seconds your jobs run.


## What minute rounding costs you


Every time a job rounds up to the next minute, you pay for compute that never ran.


Here is one pull request push: four standard jobs on a 4 vCPU / 16 GB runner, at published list rates ($0.012/min on GitHub's 4-core runner, $0.008/min normalized on StarSling):


Job Actual runtime Minute-rounded time GitHub-hosted (minute-rounded) StarSling (per-second)


Lint and format 15 s 60 s (1 min) $0.0120 $0.0020


Typecheck 45 s 60 s (1 min) $0.0120 $0.0060


Unit tests 1m 15s 120 s (2 min) $0.0240 $0.0100


Build and bundle 2m 15s 180 s (3 min) $0.0360 $0.0180


**Total per push** **4m 30s** **7m 00s** **$0.0840** **$0.0360**


The jobs ran for 4m 30s. Minute rounding bills 7 minutes, so 2m 30s of every push is padding.


Rounding costs money even at StarSling's lower rate. Billed by the minute at $0.008/min, this push would cost $0.0560. Billed by the second, it costs $0.0360. That is 36% less on this push of short jobs, before any speedup from faster hardware.


## See what you'd save


Paste this prompt into your coding agent. It reads your repository's recent GitHub Actions runs and shows how many of your billed minutes are minute-rounding padding.


Measure your minute-rounding padding Prompt for your coding agent


```text
Measure how many of this repository's billed CI minutes are minute-rounding padding.


Most CI runners bill each job from start to finish, rounded up to the next whole minute.
StarSling Runners bill by the second.
Use only the gh CLI for this. It needs no other tools or skills.


1. First, tell me this reads up to 10 workflow runs from each of the last 30 days (at most
300 runs, about 330 gh api calls) and changes nothing. Wait for my OK.
2. Then write one Python 3 script (standard library only, calling gh through subprocess),
save it to a temporary file outside the repository, and run it once. Read the owner and
repo from git remote get-url origin and put them into the API paths directly. It should:
- for each of the last 30 days, list that day's runs, 10 requests at a time:
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs?created=YYYY-MM-DD&per_page=10"
Keep the returned runs (up to 10) and that day's total_count.
- fetch each run's jobs, 10 requests at a time:
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs?per_page=100"
If a request fails, retry it once, then skip that run and count it as skipped.
- keep jobs that ended in success or failure and have both started_at and completed_at
- set aside, and count separately, jobs on labels starting with starsling- (already billed
by the second) and jobs on Windows, macOS or Arm runners (a label containing windows,
macos, arm64 or aarch64, or ending in -arm), which StarSling does not run. Count every
other job as a Linux x64 job: labels such as ubuntu-latest never say linux or x64.
- for each job: seconds = completed_at - started_at (at least 1),
billed = ceil(seconds / 60) * 60, and keep billed and actual totals per runner label, per
day and overall, so the monthly figures below come from this one run, and record each
label's runner_group_name so step 4 needs no extra API calls
- if no runs could be read or no jobs were counted, print the first error or the reason and
stop, instead of printing a report of zeros
3. Open the report with one bold line, then the details:
**Per-second billing would cut your billed CI minutes by Z%: about M minutes a month.**
- Billed today, rounded up to the minute: X minutes
- Billed by the second on StarSling: Y minutes
- Saved: X - Y minutes, which is Z% of the minutes you are billed for today
- Monthly estimate M: for each day, the minutes saved in that day's counted runs divided by
the runs counted that day, times that day's total_count; add the 30 days together. Scale
billed and actual minutes to a month the same way. Say it is an estimate.
- runs and jobs counted (and any skipped), and the 3 workflows with the most minutes saved
- if any were set aside, one line: "N jobs on Windows, macOS or Arm runners aren't included."
4. Finish by asking: "Want me to estimate how much you'd save by switching to StarSling?"
If I say yes: work out the per-minute price of the runners these jobs used from their
provider's public pricing page (ask me if you can't tell which runners or prices apply).
Read every pricing page with curl -s <url>, not a web search, so you get the live text.
Match on the hardware the jobs actually ran on (vCPU and memory), not on the label: GitHub's
standard labels such as ubuntu-latest get more vCPUs in public repositories than in private
ones, so read the size for this repository's visibility from
https://docs.github.com/api/article/body?pathname=/en/actions/reference/runners/github-hosted-runners
and GitHub's rates from
https://docs.github.com/api/article/body?pathname=/en/billing/reference/actions-runner-pricing
(the plain-text versions of GitHub's docs pages). Use the runner groups the script recorded;
do not call the API again.
With G = that size's GitHub rate and S = StarSling's rate for the same size on
https://starsling.dev/pricing.md, show a table, for the sample and scaled to a month the same
way as M, with exactly these rows:
- Today on GitHub: X x G
- Saved by per-second billing: (X - Y) x G
- Saved by StarSling's lower rate: Y x (G - S)
- On StarSling: Y x S
If the repository is public and these jobs use GitHub's standard runners, say first that
those minutes are free for public repositories, then still run the full comparison at what
a private repository would pay for runners of the same size, labeled as what a paying
repository would save.


Do not change any files.
```


## Every second you save now shows up on your bill


Modern CI runs lots of short jobs: format checks, typechecks, sharded test suites, preview deploys, and automated code reviews. Coding agents open more pull requests, so those short jobs run more often every day.


Under minute rounding, cutting a job from 1m 45s to 1m 05s still bills two minutes. Your developers wait 40 seconds less, and the invoice stays the same.


With per-second billing, speed and cost move together. Every second saved by faster CPUs,[Adaptive Compute](https://starsling.dev/blog/adaptive-compute) ,[StarSling Disks](https://starsling.dev/blog/disks) , or a merged optimization pull request from StarSling agents lowers your bill right away.


## Why we made the switch


It comes down to fairness. Rounding every CI job up to a whole minute pads the bill whenever teams run fast checks, split tests into shorter shards, or speed up their pipelines. As coding agents push more pull requests through every repository, that padding multiplies.


Per-second billing lowers our revenue per job in the short term, and it ties our revenue to making your CI fast. Charging for the exact compute you use is the right thing to do. We hope GitHub and other CI runner providers make the same change as well.
